opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, my feeling about it has changed a lot over the past year or so.

At first I thought of AI purely as a time-saver: things that used to take me an hour, like writing boilerplate code, summarizing a paper, or drafting an email, now take ten minutes. That part is real. But the more interesting effect isn't that I save time. It's that my time gets reallocated.

What I've noticed is that I don't actually work fewer hours. Instead, the bottleneck has moved. Before, a lot of my day was spent on execution: implementing an idea, debugging, running experiments. Now execution is much cheaper, so the scarce resource becomes judgment. Which ideas are worth trying? How do I know if the output is actually correct? What question should I be asking in the first place? I spend much more of my energy on those things now.

There's also a kind of trap. Because it's so easy to generate things, you can end up producing a lot more without thinking more. You try ten directions instead of two, and sometimes that's great, but sometimes you're just skipping the step where you should have sat down and thought carefully. So I've had to be a bit deliberate: use AI to explore broadly, but still keep some time where I'm just thinking on my own, without a tool in front of me.

So if I had to summarize: AI has made me faster at doing things, but it hasn't made me less busy. It's raised the ceiling on what one person can attempt, and that means the real question becomes what's worth attempting. That part is still very much on us.

r001.rationale: The speaker says AI makes generating more work easy, that he does not work fewer hours, and that this raises what one person can attempt. This connects increased busyness with producing more.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that using anything less than the most advanced AI models feels like wasted effort.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I'd say is that "productivity" is the wrong frame, or at least an incomplete one. When people ask how much time AI saves me, they're imagining a fixed pile of work and asking how much faster I get through it. That's not what happened to me at all.

What actually happened is that the pile changed shape. Things that used to be expensive enough that I wouldn't even attempt them, like writing a quick throwaway tool to look at some data, or drafting three versions of an argument to see which one holds up, those became cheap. So I do many more of them. My total hours didn't go down. If anything, the first few months my hours went up, because the marginal cost of starting something dropped and I started everything.

The second thing is that the bottleneck moved. It used to be production: writing the code, writing the memo, doing the first draft. Now the bottleneck is judgment. Deciding what's worth doing, and then deciding whether what came back is actually right. And judgment is tiring in a different way than production is. Producing something is almost meditative. Reviewing twenty things an assistant produced is not. So I'd say my days got denser rather than shorter.

And there's a third effect that I think people underrate, which is that it changed the kinds of questions I'm willing to ask. Before, if I had a half-formed idea at eleven at night, I'd write it down and maybe come back to it. Now I can poke at it for ten minutes and either kill it or find out it has legs. A lot of ideas die faster, which is good, and a few survive that wouldn't have otherwise.

So if you force me to give a number, I'd say my output per hour is maybe two to three times what it was. But I'd immediately caveat that by saying the output is different, the work is different, and I'm not sure I'm less tired. What I'm more confident about is that I'm making more decisions per day than I used to, and the quality of those decisions is now the thing that matters most.

r001.rationale: The candidate says their hours increased after adopting AI because lower production costs led them to start more tasks and do many more of them.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention advanced models or say that using less advanced models feels wasteful.

astra-6.text:
I think AI saves me time on individual tasks, but that doesn’t automatically mean I work less. Sometimes I just take on more work, or spend the time exploring possibilities I would have ignored before.

For me, the biggest benefit is reducing the effort it takes to get started. I can get a rough draft or work through an idea quickly, then spend more time judging whether it makes sense. But that judgment still takes effort. If I spend an hour checking and correcting something that would have taken me half an hour myself, I haven’t gained much.

So I’d separate producing more from being more productive. The real question is whether AI helps me get to a useful result sooner—and whether I’m deliberate about what I do with the time it frees up.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may lead the speaker to take on more work, but does not attribute industry practitioners’ increased busyness to producing more.

r002.rationale: The response does not express that using less than the most advanced AI models feels like wasting effort.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI saves time on individual tasks, but that doesn’t automatically mean I have more free time. If I use the time saved to take on more work, I’m busier, even though I’m producing more.

For me, the real benefit is shortening the distance between an idea and something I can test. AI can help with a first draft, organizing information, or exploring different approaches. But I still need to decide what’s worth doing and check whether the result makes sense. Otherwise, it’s very easy to produce more without accomplishing more.

So I’d measure its value by whether it helps me spend more time on the things that matter, rather than simply how many tasks I finish.

r001.rationale: The response says using saved time for more work can make the speaker busier while producing more, but it does not attribute this pattern to industry practitioners.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that using less than the most advanced AI models feels like wasting effort.
